# Executive Summary

## What is GLITCH

GLITCH is a research program to systematically pass a Topstep futures prop-firm evaluation (the "Combine") and then generate real payouts from the resulting funded account (the "XFA"). The project runs two parallel, independently-optimized tracks referred to throughout this report as **Cerebro 1** and **Cerebro 2**.

**Cerebro 1 — pass the Combine.** Objective: maximize the probability of reaching the profit target within a bounded ~15-day evaluation window, where the maximum loss is capped at the fee of the attempt (~$49–149). This bounded-loss, bounded-time structure permits a strategy to pass reliably even without genuine predictive edge — convexity of the payout does the work, not market prediction.

**Cerebro 2 — survive and generate payouts once funded.** A fundamentally different problem: the horizon is unbounded, there is no profit target, and the relevant threshold is 5 winning days of ≥$150 net, not a lump-sum target. A strategy with zero or negative net edge that reliably passes the Combine does **not** survive Cerebro 2 — without the bounded window protecting it, the trailing loss limit (MLL) eventually catches any strategy without genuine positive edge.

::: {.callout-important}
**Numbers that were retracted or never reproduced — stated explicitly, not omitted.** A **$134,174** payout figure appeared in an earlier Cerebro 2 analysis and was later confirmed to be **fabricated** by a prior AI session — it does not trace to any script in this repository and must never be used as a reference point. Two historical walk-forward candidates were cited with p-values of **0.149** and **0.081** — both looked like real edge, and **neither ever reproduced** when re-tested fresh in this repository (fresh reruns gave p≈0.44–0.45 for both). These two failures are the direct reason for the non-negotiable rigor standard in [Methodology & Discipline](04-metodologia-y-disciplina.qmd).
:::

## Key Findings

**Cerebro 1's G2 candidate is real, reproducible, and does not depend on predictive signal.** It exploits gambler's-ruin geometry (SL/TP placement) within the Combine's bounded-loss structure — validated against real MES price data with the triple-barrier ambiguous-bar bug fixed first (see [Cerebro 1 Timeline](01-cerebro1-timeline.qmd)).

**Cerebro 2's central structural finding: optimizing for the Combine and optimizing for XFA survival are not the same problem, and can actively conflict.** The MGC/150K candidate — designed to tolerate very few consecutive losses once funded — has a Combine pass rate of only 47.5%, roughly half of G2's 81.4%, when run through the exact same, already-audited Combine simulator. No Cerebro 2 candidate's Combine pass rate should ever be assumed from another candidate's number (see [Cerebro 2 Timeline](02-cerebro2-timeline.qmd)).

**A vectorization bug turned a ~2-hour job into a projected ~70-hour one — caught before it ran unsupervised.** An exhaustive Monte Carlo grid's ETA climbed from an estimated 2 hours to a projected 70 hours after only 1% progress; the root cause was a scalar per-path Python loop whose cost varied ~75x across the parameter space. Vectorizing it (validated bit-exact against the old implementation across 32 cases before replacing it) cut the real run to 51 minutes (see [Infrastructure & Operations](03-infraestructura-operaciones.qmd)).

**A live production incident chain cost ~2.5 weeks and traced to five distinct, unrelated root causes** — a `requirements.txt` file read from the wrong path by the actual build system in use (Railpack, not the Nixpacks config that was being edited), missing Telegram/Massive environment variables discovered one crash at a time, an ephemeral filesystem silently resetting all persistence between cron runs, and a Yahoo Finance data-availability gap at the market open (see [Infrastructure & Operations](03-infraestructura-operaciones.qmd)).

**A "10-minute" data delay claimed by a paid vendor was never verified — and a first attempt to verify it returned an impossible number, catching a second, unrelated API bug.** A real-time delay probe for Massive's futures data returned a 319,174-minute (7+ month) delay; the root cause was an unreliable API pagination pattern (`sort=asc` over a date range never returns the most recent record on this endpoint — confirmed with raw API evidence, not assumed) (see [Infrastructure & Operations](03-infraestructura-operaciones.qmd)).

## How to Read This Report

Every factual claim in this report links to a specific script, commit, or `GLITCH_RESEARCH_LOG.md` section in the [GLITCH repository](https://github.com/erictvillarreal/GLITCH) — commit-hash-pinned where precision matters, so links stay valid even as branches move or get merged. This report is a navigable index into that history, not a replacement for it: `GLITCH_RESEARCH_LOG.md` (on the `main` and `cerebro2-dev` branches — the two have not yet been merged) remains the technical source of truth. Where a number was later invalidated, contradicted, or never reproduced, this report says so explicitly next to the number, not in a separate erratum.
